title: Dancing before the ark (2 Samuel 6:12–16)
hook: the king dances with all his might, and his wife is embarrassed
tomorrow: A seat at the king's table

segments.voice: Yesterday, how are the mighty fallen: David's song for Saul and Jonathan. What good thing did you say about someone complicated? This week walked from a harp and five stones to a crown. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

Six paces. That's how far the bearers carry it before David sacrifices, oxen and fatlings, the King James says. Then the procession moves on. David is king now, and he is bringing the ark of God, the sacred chest of the covenant, up into Jerusalem, his new city. There are trumpets. There is shouting. And at the front, out ahead of everyone, the king is not walking with dignity. He's dancing. Leaping and dancing, the text says, in a plain linen garment. And above the street, at a window in the palace, one person is watching who is not dancing at all: his wife Michal, the daughter of Saul.

Here is the verse, in the King James Bible: "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod." With all his might. The King James uses the same English words for Samson bringing down the pillars, though the Hebrew behind them differs, and here they describe a king's joy. And the linen ephod matters. It was a simple linen garment, the kind the boy Samuel wore while serving at the sanctuary. The text says nothing here of a king's robe. Some readers see a king dressed for service, not for show. Then the camera moves to the window: "Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart." It's easy to make Michal the villain here, and the text is fairer than that. She loved David once. She saved his life by letting him down through a window. Then she was given to another man while David was away, and brought back to David later. Her father and brothers are dead. She has her own reasons to watch from a window. But when she meets David afterward, she mocks him for uncovering himself in front of the servant girls like a fool. And David answers: it was before the LORD. "I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight." In other words, I'll look even sillier than this if that's what worship takes. Some Christians read this chapter as permission for joy that looks undignified: hands raised, clapping, dancing in church. Others hear a quieter point about the heart: what matters is who the dance is for. Either way, the king forgot to look like a king.

Here's the practice: dance, even a little. Nobody is watching from a window. Settle, and breathe. If you can stand, stand. If not, stay where you are. Let a song you love start playing in your head, any song with joy in it. Then move something: your hands, your shoulders, your head, your feet. Small is fine. Silly is fine. Let your body be glad for a minute, without checking how it looks. If you pray, you can make it a dance before God, as David did. If you don't, let it be a dance of thanks for being alive today. The bell holds the time.
Dancing before the ark. King David, in a plain linen ephod, leaping and dancing with all his might as the ark comes to Jerusalem.
Your line: with all his might. Today, do one glad thing with all your might, and let it look a little undignified. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some churches point to David dancing before the ark when they welcome dance, clapping and raised hands in worship, while others read it mainly as a lesson about humility and the heart behind worship.

it says he was girded with a linen ephod, a plain linen garment (2 Samuel 6:14).
the text calls her Michal Saul's daughter as she watches from the window.
David apologized for how he danced
he said he would be more vile than thus, because it was before the LORD.

fork.setup: you're David. your wife says you made a fool of yourself dancing in the street. what do you say?
options: you're right. it won't happen again.
it was before the LORD, and I'll be even more undignified.
fork.reveal: "I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight." the dance was for God, not for the window.

original.note: Hebrew: ephod, a linen garment worn in the service of the sanctuary; David danced girded with one (2 Samuel 6:14).

trapdoor: what you thought: a king showing off at a parade.
what it means: David, girded in a plain linen ephod, dances before God with all his might, and won't apologize for looking foolish.
what a scholar hears: a linen ephod, a garment linked with service at the sanctuary, and Michal, Saul's daughter, with her own griefs, at the window.

notes: Week end (days 715–721): the review looks back briefly at the week (harp, five stones, crown).

'Six steps': 2 Samuel 6:13 says 'when they that bare the ark of the LORD had gone six paces, he sacrificed oxen and fatlings' (KJV). The script reads it as one stop; some read a sacrifice every six paces. Confirm phrasing.
'The same phrase the story used for Samson' (Judges 16:30, 'with all his might', day 706): the KJV uses the phrase in both; confirm the Hebrew is the same or soften to 'the same English phrase'.
The ephod: Samuel wore a linen ephod as a boy serving at Shiloh (1 Samuel 2:18). 'Linked with service at the sanctuary' is a soft summary; confirm.
Michal's history: loved David (1 Sam 18:20), saved him through a window (19:12), given to Phalti (25:44), taken back (2 Sam 3:13–16). The script avoids making her the villain; confirm tone.
David's reply to Michal paraphrased from 6:20–22; 'uncovering himself' is from 6:20. Verses 6:23 (Michal childless) omitted.
Two readings (permission for exuberant worship; the heart behind worship) attributed to 'some Christians' and 'others'.

Editor: 'an ox and a fatling' corrected to the KJV's 'oxen and fatlings' and 'six steps' to 'six paces' (6:13); 'spinning' cut (KJV 6:16 has 'leaping and dancing'); the unsourced claim that David set aside royal robes replaced with 'the text says nothing here of a king's robe' and a reading attributed to 'some readers' (1 Chronicles 15:27 does mention a robe of fine linen); myth and trapdoor adjusted to match.
Audit: the Samson link now says 'the same English words, though the Hebrew behind them differs' (2 Samuel 6:14 has be-khol oz; Judges 16:30 has be-khoach), answering the earlier note.
